title: Greedy Algorithms
tagline: The technique that builds a globally optimal solution by always making the locally best choice at each step — when it works, it works blazingly fast.

sections.content:
A **greedy algorithm** makes the locally optimal choice at each decision point and never backtracks. Where dynamic programming considers all possible subproblem combinations and picks the best, greedy simply commits to the best-looking option right now and moves on. This makes greedy algorithms typically O(n log n) or even O(n) — far faster than DP's O(n²) or O(n·W).

The challenge is knowing *when* greedy is safe. Two structural properties guarantee correctness: the **greedy choice property** (a globally optimal solution can always be reached by making a greedy local choice first) and **optimal substructure** (the optimal solution to the subproblem that remains after the greedy choice is also optimal). Classic examples include activity selection, Huffman encoding, Dijkstra's shortest path, and Prim's/Kruskal's spanning tree. The notorious counterexample is coin change with arbitrary denominations — greedy can fail spectacularly there, which is why DP is required.

sections.title: Packing a Bus With the Shortest Trips First
sections.content:
Imagine you manage a shared bus and a queue of passengers each requesting a ride of a different duration. The bus can only take one passenger at a time. You want to fit as many passengers as possible into the day.

The greedy insight: always pick the passenger whose ride ends *earliest*. Once their ride ends, the bus is free for another passenger. By greedily preferring early-finishing rides, you leave the maximum remaining time for future passengers — no DP table required. This is the **Activity Selection Problem**, and it is the canonical proof that greedy works: choosing the earliest end-time is always part of some optimal schedule, so committing to it can never prevent an optimal outcome.

**Greedy choice property** is the key structural guarantee. It means: there exists an optimal solution that includes the greedy choice we are about to make. The proof technique is an *exchange argument* — assume an optimal solution that does *not* include the greedy choice, then show you can swap in the greedy choice without making the solution worse. This argument works for activity selection (swap earliest-end for whatever the optimal solution chose first — ties or improves end time), and for Huffman coding (the two lowest-frequency symbols must be deepest in any optimal tree).

**Optimal substructure** (shared with DP) means the subproblem remaining after the greedy choice also has an optimal substructure. Once you commit the greedy choice, the rest of the problem is a smaller instance of the same problem — and solving it optimally yields a globally optimal solution.

**When greedy fails — the coin change pitfall.** With denominations [1, 3, 4] and target 6, the greedy algorithm picks 4 (largest coin ≤ 6), then 1, then 1: three coins. But the optimal solution is 3 + 3: two coins. Greedy fails because large-coin choices can block better combinations. The greedy choice property does not hold for arbitrary coin systems — you need DP.

**Huffman encoding** is a classic greedy success. To minimise total encoding bits, always merge the two lowest-frequency symbols into a single composite node, repeating until one tree remains. The exchange argument shows that the two rarest symbols must share the deepest level in any optimal prefix-free code — greedy constructs exactly that structure in O(n log n) using a min-heap.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: activitySelection sorts once by end time (O(n log n)) then makes a single linear pass — total O(n log n). The greedy invariant: after each selection, lastEnd is the earliest possible finish time for any set of non-overlapping activities chosen so far. greedyCoinChange illustrates the failure mode: with coins [1,3,4] and amount 6, it greedily takes 4 (seems best), then is forced to use two 1s — three coins total — while the optimal 3+3 uses two.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Prove greedy with an exchange argument.** To show a greedy algorithm is correct, assume an optimal solution that differs from the greedy solution at the first point of divergence. Swap the greedy choice in — show the resulting solution is no worse. If the swap never hurts, the greedy choice is always safe. If you cannot construct this argument (e.g., coin change with [1,3,4]), that is a signal to use DP instead. For fractional knapsack, sort by value/weight ratio and greedily fill — this *does* have an exchange argument. For 0/1 knapsack it does not, which is why DP is required.

items: A greedy algorithm makes the **locally optimal choice at each step** without backtracking — correct only when the problem has the **greedy choice property** and **optimal substructure**.
**Exchange argument** is the standard proof technique: assume an optimal solution that differs from greedy, swap in the greedy choice, and show the solution is no worse.
**Activity selection** (pick earliest end-time first) is the canonical greedy success: O(n log n) sort + O(n) scan finds the maximum non-overlapping set.
**Huffman encoding** greedily merges the two lowest-frequency nodes — produces a minimum expected-length prefix-free code in O(n log n) using a min-heap.
**Greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack and arbitrary coin change** — a locally large choice can block a globally better combination. Use DP when greedy's exchange argument cannot be established.

quiz.question: What two structural properties must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to guarantee a globally optimal solution?
options: Overlapping subproblems and memoisation compatibility
Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Sorted input and divide-and-conquer decomposition
Polynomial time complexity and linear space
quiz.explanation: The greedy choice property guarantees that a globally optimal solution always includes the local greedy pick (proven by exchange argument). Optimal substructure guarantees that solving the remaining subproblem optimally yields a globally optimal solution. Both are required — either alone is insufficient.

quiz.question: What is an 'exchange argument' in the context of proving greedy correctness?
options: Swapping two elements in an array to sort it in-place
Assuming an optimal solution that differs from greedy, swapping in the greedy choice, and showing the result is no worse
Exchanging the greedy algorithm for DP when greedy fails
Comparing the greedy solution against a brute-force solution on all inputs
quiz.explanation: The exchange argument is the canonical proof technique for greedy algorithms. You take any optimal solution that first diverges from the greedy solution, replace that choice with the greedy choice, and demonstrate the modified solution is still optimal. If this always holds, the greedy choice is safe.

quiz.question: The activity selection problem: given intervals [(1,4),(3,5),(0,6),(5,7),(8,11)], which set does the greedy earliest-end-time strategy select?
quiz.explanation: Sort by end time: (1,4),(3,5),(0,6),(5,7),(8,11). Greedy selects (1,4) first. Next non-overlapping: (5,7) (start 5 >= end 4). Next non-overlapping: (8,11) (start 8 >= end 7). Result: 3 activities. The alternative sets have only 2 activities.

quiz.question: Why does greedy coin change fail for denominations [1, 3, 4] with target amount 6?
options: Greedy cannot handle denominations larger than 1
Greedy picks 4, then is forced to use two 1s (3 coins) — missing the optimal 3+3 (2 coins)
The greedy algorithm does not terminate for this input
Greedy fails whenever the denomination set lacks a coin of value 2
quiz.explanation: Greedy picks the largest coin ≤ remaining amount: 4 (remaining 2), then 1 (remaining 1), then 1 (remaining 0) — 3 coins. The optimal solution is 3+3 = 2 coins. The greedy choice property fails here: choosing the largest coin first can block better combinations.

quiz.question: Which of the following problems is correctly solved by a greedy algorithm?
options: 0/1 Knapsack with arbitrary weights and values
Coin change with arbitrary denominations
Fractional Knapsack — items can be split by fraction
Longest increasing subsequence
quiz.explanation: Fractional Knapsack allows splitting items, so greedily taking items with the highest value/weight ratio first is always optimal — the exchange argument holds because fractional items can always be swapped without loss. 0/1 Knapsack, arbitrary coin change, and LIS all require DP.

quiz.question: What data structure enables Huffman encoding to run in O(n log n)?
options: Hash map for frequency lookup
Min-heap (priority queue) to always extract the two lowest-frequency nodes
Sorted array rebuilt after each merge
Binary search tree keyed on character codes
quiz.explanation: A min-heap supports extract-min in O(log n) and insert in O(log n). With n symbols, Huffman performs n-1 merges, each requiring two extract-min operations and one insert — total O(n log n). Rebuilding a sorted array after each merge would be O(n²).

quiz.question: In Huffman coding, why must the two lowest-frequency symbols be siblings at the deepest level of any optimal prefix-free tree?
options: Because the heap always places them at the bottom
Deeper nodes have longer codes — assigning the longest codes to the rarest symbols minimises total bits; any swap would increase total cost
Because prefix-free trees are always complete binary trees
The alphabet size determines tree depth independently of frequencies
quiz.explanation: Total encoding cost = sum of (frequency × code length). Deeper nodes get longer codes. To minimise cost, the symbols with highest frequency should get the shortest codes (shallowest nodes). Therefore the rarest symbols must be deepest. If they were not, swapping them with deeper symbols of higher frequency would strictly reduce total cost — contradiction with optimality.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of the activity selection algorithm (sort + greedy scan)?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n log² n)
quiz.explanation: Sorting n activities by end time costs O(n log n). The subsequent greedy scan is a single linear pass — O(n). The total is dominated by the sort: O(n log n). If the input is pre-sorted by end time, the algorithm is O(n).

quiz.question: Greedy algorithms are generally preferred over DP when applicable because:
options: They always produce the correct answer, unlike DP
They are simpler to implement and have better constant factors — O(n log n) vs DP's typical O(n²) or O(n·W)
They use less memory than DP in all cases
They work on problems without optimal substructure
quiz.explanation: When greedy is correct (exchange argument holds), it avoids the O(n²) or O(n·W) table filling of DP. Activity selection is O(n log n) greedy vs O(n²) if approached with DP. The tradeoff is that greedy is correct for a narrower class of problems — you must verify the greedy choice property first.

quiz.question: You encounter a problem: 'Select items from a list to maximise total value, where each item can be taken at most once and has a fixed weight — total weight must not exceed capacity W.' Should you use greedy or DP?
options: Greedy — sort by value/weight ratio and fill greedily
DP — this is 0/1 Knapsack, and greedy fails because items cannot be split
Either works — they produce the same result for integer weights
Greedy — sort by value descending and fill until capacity
quiz.explanation: This is the 0/1 Knapsack problem. Greedy by value/weight ratio fails because items cannot be fractioned — a high-ratio item may leave wasted capacity that prevents fitting two smaller high-value items. The exchange argument does not hold. DP with dp[i][w] or the 1D space-optimised variant is required, giving O(n·W) time.
